phases.title: Foundations
phases.description: Learn to think like a consultant — structured thinking, the MECE principle, and issue trees.

phases.title: Core Frameworks
phases.description: Master the classic strategy toolkit — 3Cs, Porter's Five Forces, BCG Growth-Share Matrix, value chain analysis.

phases.title: Problem-Solving
phases.description: Apply hypothesis-driven problem solving, master market sizing/guesstimates, and prep for case interviews.

phases.title: Client Work
phases.description: Build client-facing craft — pitch decks, top-down communication, and workshop facilitation.

phases.title: Tools
phases.description: Sharpen the hard tools — Excel modeling, PowerPoint/slide craft, and business research.

phases.title: Applied
phases.description: Practice on real material — live cases, client-style projects, and free university casebooks.

steps.d: Break down a business challenge into three mutually exclusive, exhaustive buckets that cover all possibilities.
Start with a question, split it into 2-4 child questions, then keep splitting until each leaf is answerable with data.
Take a problem breakdown and identify overlaps or gaps, then redraw it so branches don't overlap and cover everything.
Test a consulting framework (profitability, market entry, M&A) and verify that its buckets are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.
Present your issue tree to someone unfamiliar with the problem and ask them whether the splits are clear and complete.
Read a case scenario and name the primary framework a consultant would use (profitability, market entry, M&A, or pricing).
Draw a profitability framework showing revenue, COGS, operating costs, and EBITDA with annotations for where a change would hit.
Build a 3Cs (company, customer, competitor) matrix showing how your firm and rivals are positioned relative to each other.
Walk through a real or practice case about entering a new market using 3Cs, Five Forces, or go-no-go criteria.
After learning new facts during a case, modify your chosen framework and explain how your recommendation changes.
Pick an industry and assess supplier power, buyer power, threat of substitutes, threat of entrants, and competitive intensity.
For your industry, decide which one or two forces most strongly constrain profitability and explain why.
Given a proposed move (price cut, vertical integration, new market), predict how it would shift each of the five forces.
Assess two different industries side by side using Five Forces and explain which has higher structural profitability.
Find a strategic question that Five Forces alone cannot answer, then name a second framework you'd layer on top.
List your company's capabilities, constraints, and cost position relative to direct competitors.
Group customers into distinct types by size, industry, or use case and name what each segment values most.
For a direct rival, describe their positioning, cost advantage or disadvantage, and what they compete on.
Take one customer segment and explain whether your firm's current strengths align with what that segment wants most.
Propose a company-customer-competitor combination where you have a genuine advantage competitors would struggle to match.

topics.title: Estimating From First Principles
topics.description: How to build a defensible number with no data, and how to check it before someone else does.

steps.d: Start from a population and narrow it: total people → the share who qualify → how often they buy → price. Write each assumption on its own line.
Start from one unit and scale it: one outlet's daily volume → outlets in the market → days a year.
If they disagree by more than about 2x, find the assumption causing it. That assumption is the one you will be asked about.
Replace your shakiest assumption with a figure from an annual report, a census or a regulator. One real anchor makes the rest credible.
Compare the answer to something you know — a company's revenue, a city's population. If your market is bigger than the industry, start again.
Read a case scenario without looking at data and write your best guess about what's actually wrong and why.
List the specific data, metrics, or facts you'd need to confirm your hypothesis or abandon it.
Given one new piece of information, explain how your hypothesis changes and what you'd test next.
List three questions you could investigate next and pick the one that would most efficiently test your hypothesis.
Conclude the case by recommending what the client should do, rooted in which hypothesis you've narrowed down to.
Estimate a market you don't know by working up from population, consumption per person, and typical price.
Compare your estimate against known company revenues, industry reports, or GDP per capita to see whether it passes the sniff test.
After learning a new fact, recalculate your estimate and explain the delta.
Walk through your estimate with a partner and defend each assumption against their pushback or revision.
Size the same market using top-down and bottom-up methods and reconcile where they differ.
Pick a real or published case, work through it without interruption, and reach a recommendation in 30-45 minutes.
Record audio or video while you solve a case, then listen back and note where you went off track or dwelled too long.
Walk a partner through your framework for a case and ask them whether it's clear, complete, and makes sense.
Solve another case in a fixed time box—25 min for data gathering, 20 for analysis, 5 for recommendation—without exceeding it.
After finishing a case, imagine presenting to the company board and deliver your recommendation in exactly two minutes.
Take standard slide titles and rewrite them as conclusions or actions instead of topics.
Take a multi-slide deck, identify the key answer, and reorder slides to lead with the conclusion, then support it with reasons and data.
For a single idea, outline 5-7 slides with only titles and key numbers, no prose, that would answer one core question.
Check that your supporting slides don't overlap and together cover all the evidence needed for your recommendation.
Take an existing slide, identify its intended conclusion, and rewrite it so the point comes across in under three seconds.
Describe a business problem and explain your solution to the CFO in one sentence before backing into the reasoning.
Take an existing recommendation, map it to Situation-Complication-Question-Answer, and check each piece is clear.
Write a two-paragraph explanation of a finding, then condense it to one sentence plus one supporting bullet.
After presenting a recommendation, predict three questions a skeptical stakeholder would ask and draft answers to each.
Summarize a multi-week engagement for a C-level in three minutes: situation, findings, recommendation, and next steps only.
For a two-hour working session on one topic with 8-10 people, sketch timing, activities, and key decision points.
Create one five-minute brainstorm prompt that tells a small group exactly what to generate and how to report back.
Review a three-hour agenda, identify where energy will dip, and propose a change of pace or activity for each low point.
For an hour of facilitation, plan when you'll open ideas (diverge), narrow them down (converge), and move between the two.
Facilitate an actual working session, take notes on what worked and what fell flat, and write three things to improve next time.
Create an income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement linked by formulas for a company over three years.
Make three key assumptions (revenue growth, COGS %, capex) adjustable, then build sensitivity tables showing how each moves the bottom line.
Trace five calculations in a pre-built model back to source inputs and spot at least one broken formula or wrong reference.
Build base case, upside, and downside scenarios for a business and identify which would be preferred by a rational investor.
Summarize a three-statement model on one page showing key outputs and sensitivities without exposing messy calculation details.
Take a slide with five bullet points and convert it to one visual (chart, icon, or diagram) plus a headline.
For three findings (trend, comparison, part-to-whole), sketch the chart type that best shows each one.
Take a cluttered slide, snap elements to a grid, shrink fonts, and remove anything that doesn't support the headline.
Create a master slide template with company branding, text layout, and chart area, then build three content slides on top of it.
Show someone your slide for three seconds only, then ask what it's trying to say; if they hesitate, redesign it.
Locate and download the latest 10-K filing for a public company using EDGAR by company name, CIK, or ticker.
Pull revenue, net income, and operating cash flow from the consolidated statements in a 10-K.
Read the Management Discussion & Analysis section of a 10-K and write one paragraph on why earnings went up or down.
Pull financials for two competitors from their 10-Ks, calculate gross margin and ROIC, and explain who's more efficient.
Read a 10-K risk factors section and identify three material risks that could affect future earnings.
Pick one case from a Wharton, Booth, or INSEAD casebook and write a recommendation memo in 45 minutes.
After solving a case, read the official solution and note where your analysis differed from the expected approach.
Work through two related cases (both profitability, for example) and notice how the second feels easier and faster.
Submit a solved case to a coach, peer, or forum and ask for feedback on your structure, analysis, and reasoning.
After solving five cases, write one sentence for each explaining what skill or framework it was designed to teach.
Find a partner or interview service, solve a real case with someone acting as interviewer, and get real-time pushback.
Run a full 45-minute mock case interview with a partner, with video, and review the tape afterward.
After a mock interview, ask for one specific thing you did poorly and practice that weakness in a second case.
Ask your mock interviewer to push back mid-case on an assumption, and practice recovering without losing your flow.
Solve one full case per day for a week, pushing yourself to speed up and sharpen instincts on each.
